case_study_insert.main_stem: Riverlyn Retail Group (RRG) is a private limited company in the retail sector, running a chain of nine home-and-lifestyle stores and employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2011 by Daniel Rivera, the business operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. RRG plans to invest $720,000 in two new stores and a distribution centre, financed by a $300,000 bank loan and $420,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $320,000 a year, a variable cost of $9 a unit and a selling price of $25, and produces 40,000 units a year. RRG faces stock shrinkage of 5.1% of inventory and absenteeism of 8% among its store staff, which has slowed deliveries and left shelves empty at peak times in several branches.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Store Operations Report — Q3 2025: RRG sold 11,200 units across its nine stores last quarter, with stock shrinkage of 5.1% of inventory, up from 3.4% a year ago. Absenteeism reached 8% and customer complaints about empty shelves rose to 52 from 31 per month. Average checkout time was 4.1 minutes. A survey of 1,100 shoppers found 63% valued competitive prices and 46% said store layout affected their purchases. A skills audit shows 14 of 55 staff have not completed on-the-job training; off-the-job training at the local college costs $540 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Riverlyn Retail Group as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Retail Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing the cost of RRG's $300,000 variable-rate bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.9% from $13.15 to $14.06 an hour from April 2026, raising store payroll costs. (3) Wholesale input costs for home goods have risen 8.7% year-on-year, while consumer spending on homeware grew 3.9%.

questions.question_text: RRG is funding its $720,000 expansion with a $300,000 bank loan and $420,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for RRG of using retained profit rather than the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest payments or capital repayments, so RRG preserves cash while building two new stores and a distribution centre. With a $300,000 bank loan already committed and fixed costs of $320,000 a year, using the $420,000 of internal funds avoids extra debt service and leaves more of the $25 selling price to cover the $9 variable cost and absorb the 8.7% rise in wholesale input costs.

Point 2: Internal finance carries no lender covenants or collateral risk, so Daniel Rivera keeps full strategic freedom over where the two new stores open and how the distribution centre is run. It is also faster than negotiating additional borrowing, letting RRG respond to 5.1% stock shrinkage and 52 complaints about empty shelves by investing in control systems immediately rather than waiting for a bank decision. That speed protects the 63% of 1,100 surveyed shoppers who value competitive prices, since cutting shrinkage supports the low-price position without raising the $25 price during a $720,000 expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to RRG's expansion financing and operating position.

questions.question_text: RRG wants to draw shoppers to its two new stores. Consider national television advertising, local newspaper advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should RRG choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: Television can build awareness of the nine-store chain and the two new branches quickly, reinforcing the 63% of 1,100 surveyed shoppers who value competitive prices. However, airtime is costly for a retailer with $320,000 fixed costs and a $300,000 bank loan, and many viewers are outside RRG's store towns, so a large share of the spend cannot be converted into visits to the new locations.

Local newspaper advertising: Newspaper adverts with launch vouchers are cheap and can be focused on the towns around the new stores, encouraging first visits and helping shift stock affected by 5.1% shrinkage. Their limits are falling readership and a static format that cannot show store layout, which matters because 46% of surveyed shoppers said layout influences their purchases; newspapers also cannot showcase the distribution centre's faster replenishment that should reduce the 52 complaints about empty shelves.

Social media influencer marketing: Home-and-lifestyle influencers can film store tours, demonstrate the layout that 46% of shoppers care about, and announce the two new branches to a broad but relevant audience. Engagement is measurable against the 11,200-unit quarterly baseline and the 52 shelf complaints. Drawbacks are that fees vary, results build over time, and credibility depends on selecting influencers who match RRG's value positioning rather than luxury brands.

Recommendation: RRG should choose social media influencer marketing, supported by targeted local newspaper vouchers in the two launch towns. It demonstrates the store layout, reaches beyond a single newspaper catchment, and costs far less than television for a $720,000 expansion partly funded by debt. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted, while newspapers are rejected as the main channel because they cannot display the shopping experience that 46% of shoppers value. Daniel Rivera should track the 11,200-unit baseline and the 52 complaints before extending the campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to RRG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of RRG with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and newspapers are rejected.

questions.question_text: RRG's absenteeism is 8% and stock shrinkage is 5.1% under laissez-faire leadership. Explain two benefits for RRG of adopting a more democratic leadership style.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership would invite the workforce of 55, especially store assistants, to suggest how to reduce 5.1% stock shrinkage and the 52 complaints about empty shelves. Staff who handle goods daily can spot the causes of loss and propose practical stock checks; being consulted raises job satisfaction and commitment, which should reduce the 8% absenteeism that currently leaves shops understaffed.

Point 2: Involvement improves decisions because assistants know which lines run out and which displays influence the 46% of 1,100 shoppers who say layout affects purchases. Better attendance means the 4.1-minute checkout time can be maintained and the 63% who value competitive prices keep receiving good service. Moving from laissez-faire leadership to consultation also gives Daniel Rivera a way to communicate the $720,000 expansion to the workforce of 55, reducing uncertainty as two new stores and a distribution centre open and helping retain staff whose replacement costs $540 per employee in training.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RRG's absenteeism, shrinkage, complaints and expansion.

questions.question_text: RRG must train 14 of 55 staff who have not completed on-the-job training. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should RRG choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching in the stores is tailored to RRG's own stock system and checkout routines, costs no course fees, and keeps the 14 trainees productive during the 11,200-unit quarter. Supervisors can immediately address the errors behind 5.1% shrinkage and the 52 complaints about empty shelves, and link training to the 4.1-minute checkout target. Drawbacks are that senior staff lose selling time while teaching, bad habits can be passed on, and there is no external certificate for staff moving to the new stores.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $540 per employee costs 14 × $540 = $7,560, a small sum against the $720,000 investment. It provides structured retail and stock-control skills with a recognised certificate, useful as RRG opens two new stores and a distribution centre. However, it removes 14 of a workforce of 55 from the shops, risking longer checkouts and more empty-shelf complaints during an 8% absenteeism problem, and generic content must be adapted to RRG's own systems.

Decision: RRG should choose on-the-job training as the main method, adding short certified college modules for supervisors later. It is cheaper, store-specific and avoids worsening the 52 complaints while absenteeism is already 8% and the flat structure lets peers coach each other. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because $7,560 and fourteen lost shifts would disrupt the 11,200-unit operation and the new-store launch. Daniel Rivera should pilot training in one store, compare the 5.1% shrinkage figure afterwards, and only commit the $540 fee per employee where formal certification is required.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to RRG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of RRG.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and store relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how RRG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $320,000 ÷ ($25 − $9) = $320,000 ÷ $16 = 20,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 20,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $25 − $9 = $16. Answer: contribution per unit is $16.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways RRG's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 20,000-unit break-even point with output of 40,000 units gives a margin of safety of 20,000 units, showing how far sales can fall across the nine stores before RRG stops covering its $320,000 fixed costs.
2. Contribution per unit of $16 lets managers test a price promotion: cutting the $25 price by $1 to $24 leaves $15 contribution, so they can judge whether extra units from the 63% who value competitive prices offset the lower margin.
3. With a $300,000 bank loan to service and $420,000 retained profit committed, the $16 contribution and 40,000-unit output show the cash available for repayments and help phase the $720,000 spending on two new stores.
4. Unit cost can be checked as $320,000 ÷ 40,000 = $8 plus $9 variable cost = $17 a unit, letting RRG benchmark whether 5.1% shrinkage and 8% absenteeism are pushing costs above target and whether the distribution centre improves the figure.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 20,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $16 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: 20,000-unit margin of safety against 40,000 output; discount pricing from $25 using $16 contribution; servicing the $300,000 loan and $720,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $17 against shrinkage and absenteeism.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RRG's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has RRG's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 2.00 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.04 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.56 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $35,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $240,000; 2025 current assets = $185,000 + $30,000 + $40,000 = $255,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 $240,000 ÷ $120,000 = 2.00 and ($240,000 − $150,000) ÷ $120,000 = $90,000 ÷ $120,000 = 0.75. For 2025, $255,000 ÷ $125,000 = 2.04 and ($255,000 − $185,000) ÷ $125,000 = $70,000 ÷ $125,000 = 0.56.

Evaluation: The picture is mixed and the broader measure is misleading. The first figure edged up from 2.00 to 2.04, but this was driven by inventories rising from $150,000 to $185,000 while cash fell from $55,000 to $40,000 and current liabilities increased from $120,000 to $125,000. The stock-free measure fell sharply from 0.75 to 0.56, meaning RRG's liquid assets cover less of its short-term obligations. This is a concern for a retailer with $320,000 fixed costs, a $300,000 bank loan and a $720,000 expansion: the business is more dependent on selling stock that is already affected by 5.1% shrinkage and 52 empty-shelf complaints. Trade receivables improved from $35,000 to $30,000, freeing some cash, but not enough to offset the $35,000 inventory build-up and $15,000 cash fall.

Conclusion: RRG's financial position has not improved in quality. The slight rise in the broader measure is entirely inventory-led, while the stock-free measure dropped from 0.75 to 0.56, so the business is less able to meet bills without selling stock. RRG should reduce inventory and control shrinkage before funding further expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on the financial position.

questions.question_text: RRG is considering computer stock control to reduce its 5.1% shrinkage. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RRG of this approach.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Computer stock control would track inventory across the nine stores and the new distribution centre, helping pinpoint where 5.1% shrinkage occurs and reducing the 52 complaints about empty shelves. Better availability protects the $25 selling price and $16 contribution on 40,000 units, while lower losses support the 63% of 1,100 shoppers who value competitive prices during a $720,000 expansion.

Disadvantage: Installing stock-control systems needs software and staff training, adding to the $320,000 fixed costs at a time when a $300,000 bank loan is outstanding and 14 of 55 staff lack on-the-job training. The insert gives no figure for the system cost or the savings from lower shrinkage, so the net benefit cannot be quantified; the decision must be judged qualitatively. Daniel Rivera should pilot the system in one store, compare the 5.1% shrinkage and the 52 complaints, and only roll it out if the data show a clear improvement.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RRG's shrinkage, complaints, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.9% minimum wage increase and the 8.7% rise in home-goods input costs will affect RRG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If RRG's $300,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point adds 0.75% × $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 × $300,000). That is modest against fixed costs of $320,000, and a fixed-rate loan would remove it. The rise may still make future borrowing for the $720,000 expansion more expensive and could slightly dampen the 3.9% growth in homeware spending.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, to $14.06 an hour): The workforce of 55 includes many hourly-paid store staff, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided, especially with 8% absenteeism forcing cover. The insert does not state hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total would be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 40,000 units ÷ 55 staff = 727.27 units per worker, so the higher wage is sustainable only if that rate holds or improves; cutting 5.1% shrinkage and training the 14 untrained staff would help protect it.

Home-goods input costs (8.7%): These feed the $9 variable cost on every unit sold. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the full $9 were exposed, 8.7% × $9 = $0.783, about $0.78 a unit, and at 40,000 units that is roughly $31,320 a year (40,000 × $0.783). Even a smaller exposed share reduces the $16 contribution on each unit, and it recurs with every sale.

Conclusion: The 8.7% rise in home-goods input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 40,000 units and directly erodes the $16 contribution that services the $300,000 loan and funds the $720,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise costs only $2,250 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 727.27 units per worker. RRG should cut the 5.1% shrinkage and review the $25 price rather than absorb the whole increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to RRG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on RRG's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
